nv_porcelain_wall.blurb: A vertical limestone face on the east side of Mount Potosi, set just left of Clear Light Cave at the top of a steep wash walk. Every route here is bolted, and the grades lean hard: a few easier warm-ups, then a solid core of 5.10 through 5.12 with a couple of 5.13s. The stone is good quality by Potosi standards. This is mainly a winter wall because it takes the sun; in spring and fall the face drops into shade by mid-afternoon. Plan on about a mile of steady uphill walking with roughly 1,200 feet of gain, and note that the dirt road in is rough enough that a higher-clearance vehicle is the easier choice.

nv_right_north_wall.blurb: The northern wall of the Gun Club, a small limestone canyon on the western edge of the Las Vegas valley. Routes are short, mostly single-pitch sport lines on sharp, technical rock, running from beginner-friendly climbs up to low 5.12, with most of the weight between 5.8 and 5.12a and a healthy supply of 5.10s and 5.11s. The wall bakes in sun for most of the day, which makes it a good cool-weather pick and a poor summer one. It is a few minutes from the car, popular with locals, and can be busy on weekends. Handy when Red Rock sandstone is too wet to climb.
nv_right_north_wall.parking_note: The Gun Club sits behind Cliff Shadows Open Desert Park in western Las Vegas. A gravel lot and a paved lot just before it both serve the crag.
nv_right_north_wall.approach: From the lots, cross the wash to the canyon mouth straight ahead. The walk is only a few minutes.

nv_brownstone_wall.blurb: A big brown sandstone wall at the head of Juniper Canyon at Red Rock, facing east. The routes are almost all traditional, from moderate 5.7s and 5.8s up through a strong band of 5.9 to 5.11, with a few 5.12s. The long hike in, well over an hour and often closer to two, keeps crowds thin, especially midweek. Some routes sit in the sun most of the day while recessed sections stay shady. The scramble down the Gunsight, a V-shaped gully to the side, is the usual way off. Red Rock sandstone is fragile when wet, so wait for it to dry after storms.

nb_the_upper_tier.blurb: A tier of the Cochrane Lane Cliffs near Welsford, in southern New Brunswick, where steep, dark granite gives mostly single-pitch trad lines alongside a smaller number of bolted ones. Routes are short, in the range of 60 to 100 feet, and grades concentrate in the 5.10s and 5.11s with some easier and a few harder. Roof cracks and slabby sections both show up. The rock is generally solid but varies, and a few spots are flaky, so check placements. It tends to be quiet and is reached by forest trails from the road.

nb_joe_s_garage.blurb: A section of the Cochrane Lane Cliffs near Welsford, New Brunswick, made up almost entirely of traditional lines on granite. The grades spread widely, from easy 5.4 and 5.5 up to a couple of 5.13s, though the center of gravity sits in the 5.8 to 5.12 range, with plenty at 5.10 and 5.12. The cliffs overall are known for quality granite and cracks, with the odd bolted line. There is a spring directly below the wall, so keep the area clean. The cliffs are usually quiet, and on weekdays climbers can often have a section to themselves.

nb_roadside_wall.blurb: The main wall at Hampton Marsh, a rhyolite crag beside a dirt road along the water in southern New Brunswick. Almost every route is a bolted sport line, with a large block of 5.10s, a fair number of 5.9s and 5.11s, and a few 5.12s. There is essentially no approach, and the nearby harder walls, Monster and Main, are a short bushwhack up and left. Volcanic rock can break unexpectedly, so a helmet is wise, though most routes have been cleaned and feel solid. The wall dries quickly, so it works on cool days and soon after rain.

nb_evandale_quarry.blurb: An old quarry beside the highway north of the Evandale ferry in New Brunswick, with bouldering on good granite. Faces and cracks make up most of the problems, ranging from the easiest grades up to about V5, with the majority at V0 through V3. Some faces are tall, so nervous climbers may want a short top rope or extra pads for the highballs. Most walls face south, southwest or west and get sun from about nine to five in high season, with little shade, so bring sun protection for afternoon sessions.

nb_lower_tier.blurb: The lower cliff at Bear Mountain, also called Bald Hill, on granite in southern New Brunswick. It holds the province's densest cluster of hard sport routes, on horizontals, slopers and slabby, glassy faces, with a smaller handful of trad lines and one top rope. Grades center on 5.10 through 5.12 with a few easier and one 5.13. The cliff is a ten-minute or so walk from the end of a dirt track, which can be muddy after rain. The face takes sun, so it suits cooler days or morning and late-afternoon sessions, and wind can be a factor.
